description: Muslim teaching on judgment, paradise and hell, and how belief in the afterlife shapes Muslim life.
content_html:
Akhirah — Belief in Life After Death

Akhirah means “the hereafter” or life after death. It is one of the core beliefs in both Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Muslims believe that this earthly life is temporary — a test and a preparation. The real, eternal life begins after death. Everything a person does in this life will be examined on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din).

Surah 17:49–72 addresses the question of resurrection directly. The passage confronts the sceptical claim that decayed bones could not be revived, and asserts that Allah, who created humanity the first time, is entirely capable of creating again. The surah describes the journey of the soul after death, from initial disbelief through to the scales of judgement, the record of deeds and the dividing of humanity into those destined for Jannah and those for Jahannam.

Key Fact

The starred spec point (1.8*) means Akhirah is a likely anchor for 12-mark Discuss questions that ask you to compare Islamic and another tradition’s views of the afterlife. Surah 17:49–72 is the named Qur’anic anchor for Muslim teaching on resurrection and judgement.

Death and the Barzakh

After death, Muslims believe the soul enters Barzakh (the barrier or intermediate state). In Barzakh, the soul waits until the Day of Judgement. During this time, two angels — Munkar and Nakir — are believed to question the deceased about their faith. The righteous experience a peaceful Barzakh; those who have done wrong may experience suffering.

The Day of Judgement

On the Day of Judgement, the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet, all of creation will be destroyed and then all people will be resurrected. Every person will stand before Allah and give an account of their life. Islamic teaching describes several features of this judgement:

  • Each person’s deeds are recorded by the angels Kiraman Katibin (“noble scribes”) throughout their life.
  • The Mizan (scales) will weigh every person’s good and bad deeds.
  • Each person will receive a record of their deeds — in their right hand (those destined for paradise) or behind their back or in their left hand (those destined for hell).
  • The Sirat (the bridge over hell) must be crossed. The righteous cross it easily; the wicked fall into Jahannam.

Jannah — Paradise

Jannah is the Islamic concept of paradise — a place of eternal peace, beauty and fulfilment. The Qur’an describes Jannah in vivid terms: cool shade, flowing rivers, rich provision, companionship and, most importantly, the direct experience of Allah’s presence (the Beatific Vision-equivalent in Islamic theology, called ru’yat Allah). Entry to Jannah is by Allah’s mercy, not by human deeds alone — deeds are the indicator of faith, but the final decision belongs to Allah.

Jahannam — Hell

Jahannam is the Islamic concept of hell. It is described in the Qur’an as a place of fire and suffering. Muslim scholars differ on whether Jahannam is eternal for all its inhabitants. Sunni mainstream views hold that non-believers remain in hell permanently, while some Muslims who have sinned but still held faith may be punished for a time before ultimately entering Jannah by Allah’s mercy. Jahannam is not described as a place of torture for its own sake — it is described as the natural consequence of a life lived in rejection of Allah.

Belief in Akhirah motivates Muslims to act ethically in the knowledge that everything they do is being recorded. It gives purpose to suffering: if life is a test, hardship has meaning. It provides comfort in the face of death and injustice — even if wrongs are not righted in this life, they will be addressed by Allah on the Day of Judgement. It also encourages generosity and justice, since how a person treats others will be weighed on the Mizan.

This is a starred comparison spec point — examiners may ask you to compare Islamic and another tradition’s afterlife beliefs in a 12-mark Discuss question.

  • Islam: physical resurrection on the Day of Judgement; deeds weighed on the Mizan; Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell) as eternal destinations. Entry to Jannah is by Allah’s mercy. No concept of reincarnation.
  • Catholic Christianity: resurrection of the body at the Last Judgement; Purgatory as an intermediate state of purification for the faithful; Heaven, Purgatory and Hell as possible destinations. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC 1030–1032) describes Purgatory. Islam has no equivalent to Purgatory, though the concept of Barzakh shares some structural similarity as an intermediate state.
  • Hinduism/Buddhism (for contrast): reincarnation (samsara) and the eventual release from the cycle (moksha/nirvana). Islam and Christianity both reject reincarnation.
exam_tip_html: This spec point is starred (1.8*), which means it is a likely source of 12-mark Discuss questions requiring comparison with another tradition. When writing a Discuss answer on Akhirah, develop the Islamic view fully first with Surah 17:49–72 as your named anchor, then compare with Christian or another tradition’s afterlife teaching with equal depth — examiners consistently note that the “other side” is underdeveloped. The 5-mark source-of-wisdom mark: “a verse of the Qur’an” does not earn it; you need Surah 17 or a specific reference. SPaG marks: spell Akhirah, Jannah, Jahannam and Barzakh correctly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Akhirah (the afterlife) is a core Islamic belief: death is followed by Barzakh (the intermediate state), then resurrection, the Day of Judgement, and either Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell). Surah 17:49–72 is the named Qur’anic anchor for this teaching.
  • On the Day of Judgement, all deeds are weighed on the Mizan (scales); each person receives a record of their deeds. Entry to Jannah is ultimately by Allah’s mercy; Jahannam is the consequence of rejecting faith.
  • Belief in Akhirah shapes Muslim ethics, motivating good deeds and providing comfort in suffering. This is a starred spec point (1.8*) — compare Islamic afterlife belief with another tradition for the 12-mark Discuss question.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Muslim beliefs about the Day of Judgement.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: all people will be resurrected; deeds are weighed on the Mizan (scales); each person receives a book of deeds in their right (paradise) or left/behind back (hell); the Sirat bridge must be crossed; Allah gives the final verdict; the righteous enter Jannah and the wicked enter Jahannam. One mark per clearly distinct point.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims believe happens to a person after death.
practice_questions.model_answer: After death, the soul enters Barzakh (the intermediate state) where it waits for the Day of Judgement. In Barzakh, angels Munkar and Nakir question the deceased about their faith. On the Day of Judgement, all are resurrected; deeds are weighed and each person goes to Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell) according to Allah's verdict and mercy. Three descriptive points earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which belief in Akhirah influences how Muslims live today.
practice_questions.model_answer: First way: Belief in the Day of Judgement motivates ethical behaviour. Muslims believe that every deed is recorded by angels and will be weighed on the Mizan. This provides a constant incentive to act honestly, generously and justly, even when no human observer is present. Second way: Belief in Akhirah provides comfort in suffering. If this life is a test and injustice will be addressed by Allah's final judgement, then suffering in this world has meaning and wrongs will ultimately be righted. This gives Muslims resilience in the face of hardship. Two developed explanations, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Muslim beliefs about paradise (Jannah).
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First belief: Jannah is a place of eternal peace and fulfilment, described in the Qur'an as a garden with flowing rivers, abundant provision and companionship. Surah 17:49-72 addresses the resurrection that precedes entry into Jannah, stating that Allah who created humanity the first time is capable of creating again. Second belief: Entry into Jannah is ultimately by Allah's mercy, not by human deeds alone. A person's deeds are an indicator of faith, but the final decision belongs to Allah. This underlines Islamic teaching that humans are utterly dependent on divine mercy, not entitled to paradise by their own achievements. The fifth mark requires Surah 17 as the named anchor.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'Belief in life after death is the most important belief in Islam.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: Akhirah gives meaning to every aspect of Muslim life. If there is no judgement, there is no ultimate basis for ethics — why act justly if injustice goes unpunished? The Qur'an repeatedly connects moral commands to the reality of the Day of Judgement, suggesting that the afterlife is the engine of Islamic ethics. Surah 17:49-72 asserts that resurrection is as certain as the first act of creation. For millions of Muslims, the awareness of being watched and recorded gives daily life its moral seriousness. Arguments against: Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is arguably more foundational. Before any question of afterlife arises, a Muslim must believe that there is one God who created, sustains and judges. Without Tawhid, there is no framework within which Akhirah makes sense. Moreover, the Five Pillars (the practical obligations of Islam) are not primarily about preparing for death — they are about continuous submission to Allah in this life: through Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (daily prayer), Zakah (charity), Sawm (fasting) and Hajj (pilgrimage). Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that Tawhid is logically prior to Akhirah — without belief in one just God, the concept of a Day of Judgement has no force. But in terms of day-to-day impact on Muslim behaviour, belief in Akhirah is exceptionally powerful. The statement is defensible but not the only tenable position. Mastering (10-12): both sides with Qur'anic anchors; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant; vague. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of Jahannam (hell) as described in Islamic teaching.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: Jahannam is a place of fire and intense suffering; it is the destination of those who have rejected faith without repentance; the wicked fall into it when they fail to cross the Sirat bridge; some Muslim scholars distinguish between permanent inhabitants (non-believers) and temporary (sinful Muslims who may later enter Jannah by Allah's mercy); it is described as the natural consequence of a life in rejection of Allah. One mark per distinct point.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the Barzakh in Islamic belief?
options: The bridge over hell that all people must cross
The intermediate state where the soul waits between death and the Day of Judgement
The record of a person's deeds read on the Day of Judgement
The scales on which deeds are weighed at judgement

knowledge_checks.q: Which surah is the Edexcel-named Qur'anic anchor for Muslim teaching on resurrection and judgement?
In Islamic belief, the scales that weigh a person's deeds on the Day of Judgement are called the _____.
In Islam, entry into Jannah (paradise) depends ultimately on _____.
options: how many prayers a person performed
whether they performed Hajj at least once
the exact weight of their good deeds
Allah's mercy, not human deeds alone

knowledge_checks.q: Match each Islamic afterlife concept to its description:
right: Paradise — the eternal reward of the righteous
Hell — the destination of those who reject faith
The bridge over hell that all must cross on the Day of Judgement

flashcard_questions.q: What does Akhirah mean in Islam?
flashcard_questions.a: The hereafter or afterlife — life after death, the Day of Judgement and eternal destinations.
The intermediate state where the soul waits between death and the Day of Judgement.

flashcard_questions.q: Which surah addresses Muslim belief in resurrection and judgement?
What are the Mizan in Islamic belief?
flashcard_questions.a: The scales on which every person's deeds are weighed on the Day of Judgement.
The bridge over hell; the righteous cross it easily; the wicked fall into Jahannam.
Paradise in Islam — eternal peace, beauty and the presence of Allah for the righteous.
Hell in Islam — the place of punishment for those who rejected faith without repentance.

flashcard_questions.q: How does belief in Akhirah motivate ethical behaviour in Muslims?
flashcard_questions.a: Every deed is recorded and weighed; awareness of judgement incentivises just and generous living.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes the Islamic concept of Barzakh from the Catholic concept of Purgatory?
flashcard_questions.a: Barzakh is a waiting state for all; Purgatory is a purifying state for the faithful only.

flashcard_questions.q: On the Day of Judgement, how does a person know their fate in Islamic belief?
flashcard_questions.a: They receive their book of deeds — in the right hand (Jannah) or behind their back (Jahannam).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Islam reject the idea of reincarnation?
flashcard_questions.a: Islamic teaching holds there is one life, one judgement and one eternal destination — no rebirth.

glossary_terms.definition: The hereafter in Islam — the belief that there is life after death, a Day of Judgement and eternal destinations of Jannah or Jahannam.
Paradise in Islam — the eternal reward for the righteous, described as a garden of peace, beauty and the presence of Allah.
Hell in Islam — the place of punishment for those who have rejected faith without repentance.
The intermediate state between death and the Day of Judgement, where the soul waits after the body dies.
The scales on which a person's deeds are weighed on the Day of Judgement — good deeds against bad deeds.
The bridge over hell that all people must cross on the Day of Judgement — the righteous pass easily; the wicked fall into Jahannam.
Being raised from the dead on the Day of Judgement for all of humanity to stand before Allah and be judged.
